	•	macro F1 = 0.70
	•	accuracy = 0.70
	•	noise-\>platform false positives reduced from 6 to 3
	•	feature iteration should now stop
	•	the remaining issue is no longer representation quality
	•	the remaining issue is the operating point / decision policy because platform recall dropped from 0.80 to 0.70
	•	therefore the next justified move is a bounded threshold/calibration analysis, not more feature work

Do NOT change detector behavior.
Do NOT change taxonomy.
Do NOT change review labels.
Do NOT change springboard.
Do NOT add more features.
Do NOT change classifier family.

Objective

Determine whether the accepted platform_noise_feature_probe_r4 representation can be used with a different operating point that preserves platform recall at or above the required floor while keeping enough of the FP reduction to justify Phase 5 r7.

This is a platform/noise-only operating-point analysis pass.

Scope

Platform/noise only.

Keep unchanged:
	•	frozen train rows
	•	frozen holdout rows
	•	labels
	•	anchor policy
	•	classifier family
	•	accepted platform/noise r4 feature bundle
	•	springboard configuration

Do not rerun full Phase 5 in this pass.

Required outputs

Create:
	•	outputs/platform_noise_r4_operating_point_analysis.json
	•	outputs/platform_noise_r4_operating_point_analysis.md

Required work

Part A — Score-distribution analysis

Using the accepted r4 platform/noise feature bundle, inspect the score distribution on the frozen holdout.

Report:
	•	score ranges for true platform dives
	•	score ranges for true noise rows
	•	overlap region
	•	whether a better threshold than the default current one appears plausible

Part B — Threshold sweep

Run a bounded threshold sweep on the frozen holdout and report, for a useful set of thresholds:
	•	AUC (constant if applicable, but still report once)
	•	macro F1
	•	accuracy
	•	platform recall
	•	noise recall
	•	confusion matrix

Part C — Guardrail-centered operating point search

Find whether any threshold satisfies all of the following simultaneously:
	•	platform recall \>= 0.75
	•	platform/noise macro F1 \>= 0.50
	•	improved noise false positives versus r4 baseline run
	•	ideally preserves most of the AUC/ranking benefit in practical classification terms

Be explicit whether such a threshold exists.

Part D — Final decision

At the end, answer clearly with one of:
	•	PLATFORM_NOISE_R4_OPERATING_POINT_READY_FOR_PHASE5_R7
	•	STOP_AND_DOCUMENT_NEAR_PASS

Use PLATFORM_NOISE_R4_OPERATING_POINT_READY_FOR_PHASE5_R7 only if you find a threshold/operating point that makes a full r7 integration scientifically defensible.

If not, use STOP_AND_DOCUMENT_NEAR_PASS.

	•	touch springboard
	•	change labels
	•	change detector logic
	•	change taxonomy
	•	add features
	•	change model family
	•	do unrelated experiments

float((f1_platform + f1_noise) / 2.0)\n+    return {\n+        \"threshold\": round(float(threshold), 6),\n+        \"macro_f1\": macro_f1,\n+        \"accuracy\": acc,\n+ \"platform_to_noise_fn\": fn,\n+    }\n+\n+\n+def row_key_map(rows: list[dict]) -> dict[str, dict]:\n+    out: dict[str, dict] = {}\n+    counts: dict[str, int] = {}\n+    for row in rows:\n+        sid = str(row[\"source_session_id\"])\n+        counts[sid] = counts.get(sid, 0) + 1\n+        cid = row.get(\"legacy_candidate_id\")\n+        rid = str(cid) if cid else f\"row-{counts[sid]:04d}\"\n+        out[f\"{sid}::{rid}\"] = row\n+    return out\n+\n+\n+def write_md(report: dict) -> None:\n+    lines = [\n+        \"# Platform/Noise r4 Operating-Point Analysis\",\n+        \"\",\n+        f\"- decision: `{report['decision']}`\",\n+        \"\",\n+        \"## Part A — Score distribution\",\n+        \"\",\n+        f\"- true platform score range: `{report['part_a_score_distribution']['platform_score_range']}`\",\n+        f\"- true noise score range: `{report['part_a_score_distribution']['noise_score_range']}`\",\n+        f\"- overlap region: \"\",\n+        \"## Part B — Threshold sweep\",\n+        \"\",\n+        f\"- AUC (ranking, threshold-invariant): `{report['part_b_threshold_sweep']['auc']:.4f}`\",\n+        \"\",\n+        \"| threshold | macro F1 | accuracy | platform recall | noise recall | confusion matrix |\",\n+        \"|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---|\",\n+    ]\n+    for row in Guardrail search\",\n+            \"\",\n+            f\"- constraint platform recall >= 0.75: `{report['part_c_guardrail_search']['constraint_platform_recall_floor']}`\",\n+            f\"- constraint macro F1 >= 0.50: `{report['part_c_guardrail_search']['constraint_macro_f1_floor']}`\",\n+            f\"- constraint noise FP improved vs r4 baseline (3): \"\",\n+            \"## Part D — Final decision\",\n+            \"\",\n+            f\"- `{report['decision']}`\",\n+            f\"- rationale: `{report['decision_rationale']}`\",\n+            \"\",\n+        ]\n+    )\n+    OUT_MD.write_text(\"\\n\".join(lines))\n+\n+\n+def main() -> None:\n+    r4 = json.loads(R4_PATH.read_text())\n+    r4_baseline_fp = row_key_map(rows)\n+    lists = json.loads(LISTS_PATH.read_text())\n+\n+    train = [RowRef(item[\"row_key\"], item[\"event_label\"], by_key[item[\"row_key\"]]) for item in lists[\"platform_noise_track\"][\"train_rows\"]]\n+    holdout = [RowRef(item[\"row_key\"], item[\"event_label\"], by_key[item[\"row_key\"]]) for item in lists[\"platform_noise_track\"][\"holdout_rows\"]]\n+\n+    audio_cache: dict[str, np.ndarray] = {}\n+    fmap: dict[str, dict[str, float]] = {}\n+    for item in train + holdout:\n+        sid =       end = max(start + 0.05, to_float(item.row.get(\"event_window_end_seconds\")))\n+        s0 = int(round(start * SAMPLE_RATE))\n+        s1 = int(round(end * SAMPLE_RATE))\n+        fmap[item.row_key] = extract_features(signal[s0:s1], sample_rate=SAMPLE_RATE)\n+\n+    def vec(item: RowRef) -> list[float]:\n+        row = item.row\n+        return [\n+            to_float(row.get(\"audio_score\")),\n+            to_float(row.get(\"audio_clip_probability\")),\n+            to_float(row.get(\"event_anchor_timestamp_seconds\")),\n+            1.0 if row.get(\"is_false_negative_window\") else 0.0,\n+            *[to_float(fmap[item.row_key][name]) for name in PROBE1_FEATURE_NAMES],\n+            *[to_float(fmap[item.row_key][name]) for name in row\n+        for row in threshold_results\n+        if row[\"platform_dive_recall\"] >= 0.75\n+        and row[\"macro_f1\"] >= 0.50\n+        and row[\"noise_to_platform_fp\"] < r4_baseline_fp\n+    ]\n+\n+    best_candidate = None\n+    if feasible:\n+        feasible_sorted = sorted(\n+            feasible,\n+            key=lambda row: (-row[\"macro_f1\"], -row[\"accuracy\"], row[\"noise_to_platform_fp\"], row[\"platform_to_noise_fn\"]),\n+        )\n+        best_candidate = feasible_sorted[0]\n+    else:\n+        # Closest non-feasible point: maximize platform recall,     row[\"noise_to_platform_fp\"],\n+                -row[\"macro_f1\"],\n+                -row[\"accuracy\"],\n+            ),\n+        )\n+        best_candidate = non_sorted[0]\n+\n+    decision = Goal of the document

The goal is not to run all experiments now.

5. incorporates relevant external research / community practice where useful
6. states what evidence each experiment is meant to produce
7. defines decision rules for moving forward or stopping
8. is directly actionable by future agents without context drift

1. # DiveSensei Detector Status
2. 
3. Date: 2026-04-11
4. 
5. This document freezes the current detector state, the validated research outcomes, and the lines of work that are closed.
6. 
7. ## 1. Current Validated Detector
8. 
9. The production reference detector is the validated region-tie-break branch:
10. 
11. - `frontend_region_descriptor_enabled`
12. - `frontend_region_descriptor_pattern_tiebreak_band = 0.20`
13. - `frontend_region_pattern_exception`
14. - `frontend_dense_pcen_pattern_exception`
15. - `frontend_region_tail_imbalance_exception`
16. 
17. This is the last fully validated, stable, cross-session-safe detector.
18. 
19. Validated properties:
20. 
21. - stable on INSEP and Champigny
22. - stable replay coverage
23. - stable FP/min
24. - recovered `48.656411s`
25. - recovered `417.488888s`
26. - preserved `114.350347s` as an evaluation/accounting artifact recovery
27. 
28. ## 2. Experimental Branches
29. 
30. The only remaining experimental branch to keep around is:
31. 
32. - `frontend_short_region_tail_exception`
33. 
34. Status:
35. 
36. - useful local movement on `145.714040s`
37. - no regression in the session where it first helped
38. - did not generalize on the springboard-heavy `insep_15min.mov` validation session
39. 
40. Interpretation:
41. 
42. - experimental only
43. - session-specific
44. - not promoted to default
45. 
46. ## 3. Springboard Failure Analysis
47. 
48. The springboard-heavy session showed a different confuser regime from platform INSEP:
49. 
50. - board rebounds dominate the false-positive landscape
51. - voice / whistle / clap-like events are common
52. - many false negatives are close misses where the detector lands on the last rebound rather than the splash
53. 
54. The key result from that session:
55. 
56. - peak-first selection is structurally insufficient in rebound-heavy clusters
57. - event-level structure helps offline, but cannot be safely dropped into the live peak-first funnel
58. 
59. ## 4. Rebound Discrimination Research
60. 
61. Offline event-level modeling was meaningful:
62. 
63. - dive vs rebound separation improved materially
64. - cluster ranking improved on average
65. - the event-level score could distinguish structured dive-like windows from rebound-like windows better than peak-only selection
66. 
67. However:
68. 
69. - event-level scoring alone did not create top-1 recoveries
70. - the live detector still needs a safe decision boundary
71. 
72. ## 5. Event-Level Modeling Research
73. 
74. The offline research answered a narrow but important question:
75. 
76. - yes, event-level structure is real
77. - yes, it is better than peak-only ranking for some springboard clusters
78. - no, it is not directly compatible with the current detector funnel
79. 
80. The validated conclusion is architectural:
81. 
82. - event-level modeling improves dive vs rebound separation offline
83. - event-level modeling improves cluster ranking offline
84. - event-level modeling cannot be safely integrated as a local peak replacement inside the current detector
85. 
86. ## 6. Integration Attempts And Failures
87. 
88. All of the following are closed:
89. 
90. - event-level reranking
91. - event-level score blending
92. - representative selection
93. - delayed cluster selection
94. - cluster winner replacement
95. - merge-stage event veto
96. 
97. Observed failure modes:
98. 
99. - candidate collapse
100. - replay degradation
101. - loss of accepted detections
102. - no measurable gain in live detector conditions
103. 
104. The repeated lesson:
105. 
106. - local cluster modifications are not safe injection points in the current peak-first funnel
107. - the funnel is tightly coupled to suppression, merge, and ranking dynamics
108. 
109. ## 7. Final Architectural Conclusion
110. 
111. The limitation is architectural, not feature quality.
112. 
113. The current detector assumes:
114. 
115. - event equals best peak
116. 
117. That is wrong for springboard rebound-heavy sessions.
118. 
119. But the live funnel cannot be lightly changed by swapping winners or adding local vetoes because:
120. 
121. - suppression changes candidate survival
122. - merge changes the candidate set
123. - ranking changes who survives later gates
124. 
125. So the right conclusion is:
126. 
127. - event-level reasoning is valid
128. - the current peak-first detector is not the right architecture for direct event-level insertion
129. - a new event-aware pipeline would need a cleaner boundary than local peak modification
130. 
131. ## 8. Recommended Future Directions
132. 
133. Use the validated branch as the default baseline.
134. 
135. Treat event-level work as a separate future architecture line, not a detector patch.
136. 
137. The next detector-side work that remains plausible is:
138. 
139. - springboard-heavy below-threshold misses
140. - pre-candidate capping / suppression
141. - rebound-heavy confuser analysis
142. 
143. Do not continue to stack failed event-integration heuristics.
144. Do not revisit solved or ambiguity cases as if they were unresolved detector misses.
145. 
146.
```

1. # Handoff — 2026-04-13 Near-Pass Closure
2. 
3. This cycle is closed as a **near-pass** with no further experiments in-pass.
4. 
5. ## Fixed conclusions at closure
6. 
7. - Springboard is a real pass and remains frozen (`probe_r1_only`).
8. - Platform/noise improved substantially with accepted representation work.
9. - Accepted r4 platform/noise bundle produced strong ranking signal (`AUC=0.81`) and improved noise false positives (`6 -> 3` vs accepted r2 result).
10. - Under current constraints, platform recall and noise false-positive guardrails cannot be satisfied simultaneously by threshold tuning alone.
11. - Therefore, feature micro-iteration and threshold micro-iteration stop here.
12. 
13. ## Best-known current state
14. 
15. - Detector behavior: frozen validated detector (proposal generator only).
16. - Taxonomy/labels: unchanged.
17. - Classifier family: unchanged logistic family.
18. - Platform/noise representation: accepted r4 4-feature bundle.
19. - Global status: **near-pass / not full pass**.
20. 
21. ## Why no further in-cycle work
22. 
23. - The current gap is a constrained operating-policy tradeoff, not missing obvious signal.
24. - Additional tiny tweaks are not the highest-value next action.
25. 
26. ## Next cycle (explicitly out of scope for this pass)
27. 
28. 1. Evaluate stronger platform/noise model family.
29. 2. Add cleaner/more platform-noise data for ambiguous residual clusters.

<details>
<summary>113 lines</summary>

```
1. # Phase 4 To Now Recap
2. 
3. Date: 2026-04-13
4. 
5. ## Current State
6. 
7. The project is now in the event-window / event-review phase transition.
8. 
9. What is stable:
10. 
11. - the validated legacy detector remains frozen
12. - the review UI now supports event-review suggestions and human event labels
13. - reviewed event manifests can be exported separately from legacy detector labels
14. - the reviewed dataset summary pipeline is in place
15. - a simple offline event-classifier baseline exists
16. 
17. What is not yet stable:
18. 
19. - the full four-class event model is still not stable enough for Phase 5 simulation
20. - `springboard_dive` still collapses into `springboard_rebound_only` in the full reviewed baseline
21. - the current anchor/window policy is only partially sufficient
22. 
23. ## Phase 4 Path
24. 
25. Phase 4 established the first usable offline baseline for the new taxonomy.
26. 
27. Observed results from the reviewed-label baseline:
28. 
29. - `platform_dive` vs `noise_or_other` became meaningfully learnable
30. - `springboard_dive` vs `springboard_rebound_only` remained weak under the original proposal-centered representation
31. - the four-class prototype remained unstable
32. 
33. That led to a stop decision rather than moving into Phase 5.
34. 
35. ## Springboard-Specific Finding
36. 
37. The springboard failure analysis showed:
38. 
39. - proposal-centered windows were the wrong primary representation for springboard events
40. - the 3.0s window length was not the main problem
41. - `earliest_strong_peak_in_local_cluster` was the best springboard anchor tested
42. - a delayed-entry-centered proxy was weaker and less stable
43. 
44. The springboard-only experiment then confirmed:
45. 
46. - springboard became substantially more learnable when the anchor shifted to the earliest strong peak proxy
47. - the anchor choice mattered more than small window-length tweaks
48. 
49. ## Manifest Policy Update
50. 
51. The manifest/export layer was updated so anchor policy is conditional by regime:
52. 
53. - springboard rows use `earliest_strong_peak_in_local_cluster`
54. - platform rows remain `proposal_centered`
55. 
56. This policy is explicit in the exported artifacts via:
57. 
58. - `event_anchor_strategy`
59. - `event_anchor_strategy_rationale`
60. 
61. However, when the full reviewed four-class baseline was rerun with the updated policy, the aggregate metrics did not materially change. That means the representation fix alone is not enough to justify simulation yet.
62. 
63. ## UI / Workflow Status
64. 
65. The desktop review app now includes:
66. 
67. - event-review suggestions
68. - editable human event labels
69. - a refinement queue for high-value rows
70. - explicit handling for manual false-negative review rows
71. - a more compact review sidebar
72. 
73. The UI also had multiple real regressions that were fixed along the way:
74. 
75. - false-negative markers disappeared from the timeline and had to be reintroduced
76. - the refinement queue duplicated the old review list and had to be simplified
77. - the save path for event labels needed multiple passes to persist correctly
78. - false-negative rows required special handling so they behaved like first-class review items
79. 
80. These were workflow issues, not detector issues.
81. 
82. ## Main Struggles
83. 
84. The main blockers encountered were:
85. 
86. 1. `springboard_dive` remained hard to separate from `springboard_rebound_only`
87. 2. session context mattered more than the initial manifest policy assumed
88. 3. the review UI had several persistence and layout edge cases
89. 4. the full four-class baseline still did not recover a stable decision boundary even after better springboard anchoring
90. 
91. ## Current Conclusion
92. 
93. The project is still in a refinement phase.
94. 
95. Accepted conclusions:
96. 
97. - keep the validated detector frozen
98. - keep the new taxonomy and event-review workflow
99. - keep the conditional anchor policy in the manifest layer
100. - do not start Phase 5 simulation yet
101. - do not add model capacity yet
102. - do not broaden relabeling until the remaining confusion rows are prioritized again
103. 
104. ## Ongoing Direction
105. 
106. The next useful work is still constrained:
107. 
108. - continue using the new review workflow
109. - keep the reviewed artifacts fresh
110. - inspect only targeted confusion-driving rows
111. - avoid another broad architecture jump until the springboard boundary is actually stable in the full four-class setting
112. 
113.
```

</details>

1. # Phase 5 Final Status (Current Cycle Closure)
2. 
3. ## Part A — Final status
4. 
5. - **Springboard track:** pass (stable, accepted, unchanged in this cycle)
6. - **Platform/noise track:** near-pass under current constraints; fails current joint recall/FP guardrail requirement
7. - **Global Phase 5:** near-pass / not fully passed
8. 
9. ## Part B — Best-known configuration (frozen)
10. 
11. - **Detector line:** frozen validated detector as proposal generator only  
12.   (`frontend_region_pattern_exception`, `frontend_dense_pcen_pattern_exception`, `frontend_region_tail_imbalance_exception`)
13. - **Springboard feature family:** `probe_r1_only` (accepted best, no regression)
14. - **Platform/noise feature family (representation):** accepted `platform_noise_feature_probe_r4` bundle  
15.   (`spectral_contrast_mean_post`, `spectral_contrast_low_high_slope_post`, `onset_tempogram_peak_ratio_post`, `onset_density_0_300ms_post`)
16. - **Classifier family:** unchanged logistic model family
17. - **Validation policy:** frozen manifest/slice structure (platform/noise 20-row scored holdout: 10 platform, 10 noise)
18. 
19. Best observed platform/noise results with accepted r4 representation:
20. 
21. - **AUC:** 0.81
22. - **Macro F1:** 0.70
23. - **Accuracy:** 0.70
24. - **Confusion:** `[[7, 3], [3, 7]]`
25. - **Noise->Platform FP:** 3 (improved from 6 in accepted r2 run)
26. - **Platform recall:** 0.70 (down from 0.80 in accepted r2 run)
27. 
28. Operating-point analysis outcome:
29. 
30. - Threshold tuning changes precision/recall tradeoff, but no threshold satisfied all required constraints simultaneously:
31.   - platform recall >= 0.75
32.   - macro F1 >= 0.50
33.   - strict noise->platform FP improvement vs r4 default operating point
34. 
35. ## Part C — Why this cycle stops here
36. 
37. - The remaining blocker is no longer weak representation signal (AUC is strong at 0.81).
38. - The blocker is decision-policy geometry under current constraints: improving recall reintroduces too many noise false positives; reducing false positives drops platform recall below floor.
39. - Additional tiny feature or threshold tweaks are unlikely to change this structural tradeoff enough to justify continued micro-iteration in this cycle.
40. - This is a constrained **near-pass**, not a broad failure.
41. 
42. ## Part D — Next-cycle options (ranked; not for this pass)
43. 
44. 1. **Stronger platform/noise model family:** move beyond current logistic family while keeping detector/taxonomy/labels frozen.
45. 2. **More/cleaner platform-noise data:** expand and clean ambiguous handling/whistle/noise rows and boundary platform rows.
46. 3. **Protocol/governance decision:** explicit policy on track-level acceptance vs strict global acceptance.
47. 4. **Calibration/governed deployment mode:** if governance allows, adopt confidence-banded review policy rather than single hard threshold.
48.

1. # Next-cycle research plan to improve platform/noise performance in the Phase 5 regime-aware pipeline
2. 
3. ## Executive summary
4. 
5. Your current platform/noise failure mode is *not* a simple label/taxonomy issue; it is a mixed negative-cluster separation problem dominated by handling-like clutter and whistle/voice-like tonal artifacts, which previously collapsed into “platform” without enough discriminative cues. The internal frozen-slice diagnosis explicitly shows this mixed cluster structure and points to “insufficient event-shape distinction” as the top-ranked root cause. fileciteturn0file2 The complementary feature-family design document (from the same cycle) frames the repair as compactness/decay/texture/isolation features, i.e., “shape/texture discrimination” rather than detector or taxonomy changes. fileciteturn0file0
6. 
7. Next cycle, the highest-leverage opportunities are now *beyond* hand-crafted scalar tweaks. You want methods that (a) learn non-linear interactions among your best features, (b) import robust audio semantics via pretraining, and (c) explicitly optimize a ranking-aware objective (because ROC AUC is fundamentally a ranking measure). AUC’s interpretation as a probability of correctly ranking a random positive above a random negative can be formalized via its equivalence to rank-based statistics (Mann–Whitney U), which is why rank-focused training often helps when you’re “close” on AUC. citeturn8search0turn8search8
8. 
9. ### Prioritized short list
10. 
11. **Top candidate**  
12. Adopt a non-linear tabular model on the existing (fixed) platform/noise feature set, with an AUC-first validation protocol: gradient boosted decision trees (GBDT) and/or a small ranking objective variant. GBDT toolchains are mature (e.g., entity["organization","XGBoost","gradient boosting library"] and entity["organization","LightGBM","gradient boosting library"]), and both expose AUC directly, with ranking objectives available when you want to train explicitly for ordered separation. citeturn7search0turn1search0turn20search0turn8search2  
13. **Expected benefit:** improved AUC and more flexible FP/FN tradeoff via feature interactions.  
14. **Effort:** low→medium (mostly plumbing + careful CV).  
15. 
16. **Second candidate**  
17. Evaluate pretrained audio embeddings (extract once, then keep the classifier shallow), then train a small classifier on top (logistic/GBDT). The OpenL3 and PANNs lines are explicitly motivated for “small labeled downstream datasets via embeddings,” which matches your constraints. citeturn10search0turn3search0turn3search14  
18. **Expected benefit:** large lift in robustness/generalization on heterogeneous noise modes.  
19. **Effort:** medium (dependency + batching + reproducibility).  
20. 
21. **Third candidate**  
22. Introduce semi-supervised consistency/pseudo-label training and/or mixed-sample augmentation applied at the spectrogram level, targeting your “heterogeneous negative modes” and the under-covered edge cluster. DCASE Task 4 baselines (domestic sound event detection) use semi-supervised Mean Teacher recipe patterns, demonstrating practical value under weak/strong/unlabeled mix regimes. citeturn14search3turn14search0turn10search2  
23. **Expected benefit:** increases effective data size and reduces variance; likely improves tail performance.  
24. **Effort:** medium→high (pipeline complexity and leakage risk).
25. 
26. ### Longer list to keep in scope, but not first
27. 
28. Time–frequency scattering features (stable, small-data friendly), entity["organization","Kymatio","scattering transforms library"]-based. citeturn0search7turn16search12turn16search3  
29. Learnable front-ends (LEAF, SincNet-style), when you can afford iterative neural training. citeturn15search0turn15search1  
30. Metric-learning / few-shot framing (Prototypical Networks) if you want device/session invariance and cluster separation without heavy label volume. citeturn17search0turn17search2  
31. Governance changes: confidence intervals and guardband policies based on uncertainty, especially when holdouts are small (DeLong CI, bootstrap). citeturn11search2turn11search1
32. 
33. ## System frame and technical constraints
34. 
35. This plan assumes you will keep the following fixed unless explicitly stated otherwise:
36. 
37. The detector remains frozen as a proposal generator (no detector retraining).  
38. Springboard remains frozen at **probe_r1_only** (no springboard feature changes).  
39. Labels and slice definitions are treated as “fixed for this cycle,” but the next cycle can *add* new reviewed holdouts (governance item) while preserving comparability.  
40. The current classifier family is `numpy_logistic_regression_binary` (preferred to keep), but evaluation will explicitly compare against stronger families as next-cycle options.
41. 
42. ### Why the platform/noise case is structurally hard
43. 
44. The internal analysis shows a 20-row balanced, proposal-centered platform/noise scored slice, where (a) false positives are dominated by “handling_noise” and “voice_whistle,” and (b) the ranked diagnosis prioritizes missing event-shape/texture discrimination over label ambiguity. fileciteturn0file2 This is an archetypal “mixed negative manifold” problem: multiple acoustic mechanisms land near the same decision region unless the representation has (or learns) enough separation axes.
45. 
46. That is exactly the regime where either (i) non-linear interaction models, (ii) pretrained embeddings, or (iii) semi-supervised regularization provide disproportionate benefit relative to “one more scalar feature.”
47. 
48. ## Model-family options for small-data audio ranking
49. 
50. ### Comparison table of candidate model families
51. 
52. | Model family | Rationale for your regime | Expected benefit | Required code/data changes | Effort | Common failure modes | Success measurement |
53. |---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
54. | Regularized logistic (keep baseline) using entity["organization","scikit-learn","python ml library"] logistic tooling | Strong baseline; regularization built-in; stable with tiny data. citeturn21search3turn6search2 | Better weight stability; can add class weights; easy calibration | Swap/augment numpy solver with scikit estimator; add CV and persistence | Low | Still linear; cannot fit feature interactions; can underfit mixed cluster | AUC and guardband thresholds; bootstrap CI for AUC |
55. | Calibrated logistic (Platt / isotonic / temperature) | Post-hoc probability calibration improves decision use; calibration methods are standard. citeturn0search4turn12search2turn13search0 | Better probability meaning; may improve operating point; rarely changes AUC much | Add calibration step; store calibrator; separate calibration fold | Low→Med | Overfitting calibrator on tiny calibration sets; “looks better” but doesn’t generalize | Brier score + calibration curves; must still pass AUC/floor metrics citeturn21search1turn0search4 |
56. | GBDT classifier (tree boosting) | Strong performance on tabular features; learns interactions without deep nets. Core systems: LightGBM/XGBoost papers + docs. citeturn1search0turn7search0turn1search16 | Likely AUC boost; can reduce residual FP cluster via interactions | Add training wrapper, feature importance interpretability; tune with nested CV | Low→Med | Overfitting if too many trees/depth; leakage if CV not strict | AUC + macro F1 + recall/FP guardrails on fixed slice |
57. | Pairwise learning-to-rank (LTR) objective on tabular features | AUC is a ranking measure; pairwise objectives explicitly optimize ordering. XGBoost ranking tutorial + AUC note in params. citeturn8search2turn8search17 | Directly targets ranking overlap; may lift AUC | Map your binary dataset to single-group ranking problem; add LTR dataset builder | Med | “Group” semantics mismatch; instability with tiny n; engineering overhead | AUC improvement with CI; check no platform recall collapse |

62. 
63. ### Practical guidance on model-family selection
64. 
65. GBDT is the lowest-friction “step up” from linear models because it directly models feature interactions (e.g., spectral contrast × onset density × decay ratios) without requiring neural training pipelines. The core algorithmic references for modern boosting implementations are the XGBoost and LightGBM system papers. citeturn7search4turn1search16
66. 
67. If you want a ranking-aware approach: note that XGBoost explicitly documents learning-to-rank and recognizes AUC in LTR settings as pairwise-comparison-based. citeturn8search2turn8search17 This is conceptually aligned with your “residual overlap in score ordering” diagnosis, because AUC directly measures ranking correctness (probability positive outranks negative). citeturn8search8turn8search4
68. 
69. ## Representation, augmentation, and semi-supervised options
70. 
71. ### Representation strategies beyond the current bundle
72. 
73. Your last-cycle docs already made a correct move: move from generic features to compactness/decay/texture/isolation cues. fileciteturn0file0 Next-cycle representation work should focus on *reusable* and *robust* representations rather than incremental ad hoc scalars.
74. 
75. #### Pretrained embedding families
76. 
77. PANNs explicitly targets transfer to multiple downstream audio tasks after AudioSet pretraining, with released models and code. citeturn3search0turn3search20  
78. YAMNet is readily usable as a pretrained AudioSet classifier backbone for embeddings. citeturn3search1turn3search5  
79. OpenL3 is explicitly motivated by learning embeddings usable for small labeled tasks. citeturn10search0turn3search14  
80. CLAP provides audio embeddings aligned to language supervision; you can use it purely as an audio encoder for downstream classification even without text. citeturn19search0turn19search8
81. 
82. A key practical advantage: you can freeze the embedder and keep your “small-data head” simple (logistic or boosting). This reduces cycle time and makes analysis more interpretable (you can attribute improvements to representation, not a complex end-to-end training story).
83. 
84. #### Learnable front-ends and end-to-end spectral training
85. 
86. LEAF demonstrates a lightweight learnable replacement for mel filterbanks, aiming to outperform fixed mel features across multiple audio tasks. citeturn15search0turn15search16  
87. SincNet imposes inductive bias in the first layer via parametrized band-pass filters and can converge faster with interpretable filters. citeturn15search1turn15search5
88. 
89. These are powerful, but they are higher risk for your case unless you have (or can create) more labeled data, because end-to-end audio models can overfit small datasets unless heavily regularized.
90. 
91. #### Time–frequency scattering and wavelet-based features
92. 
93. Time–frequency scattering work (Mallat/Andén/Lostanlen line) offers stable representations for audio classification, designed for invariance and robustness. citeturn0search7turn16search3  
94. Kymatio provides a modern scattering transform implementation and positions scattering as stable to additive noise with variance reduction—directly relevant to “handling/noise clutter” robustness. citeturn16search3turn16search12
95. 
96. This is an attractive mid-point: more principled than ad hoc features, less training-heavy than deep nets.
97. 
98. ### Data augmentation and semi-supervised learning
99. 
100. #### Augmentation recipes with evidence in audio tasks
101. 
102. SpecAugment (time/frequency masking) is widely used and documented, and is implemented directly in audio libraries (e.g., torchaudio transforms include SpecAugment masking ops). citeturn0search1turn15search3  
103. SpecMix proposes mixed-sample augmentation via time-frequency masks, aimed at preserving spectral correlation while mixing samples, with reported improvements across audio tasks. citeturn9search7turn9search8  
104. Audio mixup variants appear in DCASE workshop work targeting small datasets where overfitting is common. citeturn9search12turn2search0
105. 
106. For your use case: apply augmentation *before* feature extraction (or on spectrograms if using CNN/embeddings). Mixed-sample augmentation is particularly plausible if your dominant errors are “negative looks positive”: mixing can help teach smoother boundaries by generating hard intermediates.
107. 
108. #### Semi-supervised recipes that fit your domain
109. 
110. Mean Teacher is a standard consistency-regularized semi-supervised method. citeturn14search0turn14search4 DCASE domestic SED baselines explicitly use a mean-teacher model recipe (in that task family). citeturn14search3turn10search2  
111. FixMatch provides an alternative pseudo-label + strong augmentation approach: generate pseudo-labels from weak aug predictions, then enforce consistency on strong aug variants. citeturn2search1turn2search5  
112. Classic pseudo-labeling (pick max-prob class for unlabeled points) is simpler but higher risk for confirmation bias. citeturn2search15
113. 
114. For your pipeline: you likely have abundant *unlabeled proposals* (detector outputs) even if reviewed labels are scarce. Semi-supervised approaches exploit exactly that condition, but only if leakage control is strict.
115. 
116. ### Practical libraries for augmentation and feature extraction
117. 
118. If you adopt neural training, the augmentation ecosystem is strong: audiomentations (CPU) and torch-audiomentations (GPU) provide ready-to-use transforms. citeturn16search0turn16search1  
119. For feature computation consistency, librosa provides spectral contrast and onset/tempogram building blocks. citeturn5search0turn5search2turn5search3  
120. Essentia provides spectral contrast and many other MIR features but is AGPL by default, which can be a licensing risk depending on your distribution model. citeturn5search1turn22search0
121. 
122. ## Calibration and operating-point methods
123. 
124. ### What calibration can and cannot fix
125. 
126. Calibration improves the *meaning* of predicted probabilities (reliability), not necessarily the rank ordering. Temperature scaling (a single-parameter Platt variant) is reported to be surprisingly effective for neural nets in many settings. citeturn13search0turn13search4  
127. The scikit-learn calibration guide describes Platt-style sigmoid and isotonic calibration workflows and provides a canonical implementation route. citeturn0search4turn0search0  
128. Brier score is a proper scoring rule for probability quality and is implemented directly as `brier_score_loss`. citeturn21search1turn12search7
129. 
130. Given your recent finding that “no threshold satisfies recall floor + FP improvement simultaneously,” calibration alone may not be enough. But calibration can still be valuable in two next-cycle situations:
131. 
132. If you move to non-linear models that produce miscalibrated probabilities (boosting is often miscalibrated), then calibrated post-processing can restore decision stability without changing rank much. citeturn12search2turn0search4  
133. If governance allows a constrained operating-point search (see below), calibrated scores make the constraint search more interpretable and stable.
134. 
135. ### Constrained decision policies and asymmetric-risk optimization
136. 
137. If platform recall must be above a floor (e.g., ≥ 0.75) while also controlling FP, this is naturally a constrained optimization / Neyman–Pearson style problem: minimize one error subject to controlling the other. Classic Neyman–Pearson classification literature and more recent rate-constrained optimization work formalize this view. citeturn6search8turn6search5
138. 
139. Practically, you can implement this next cycle as:
140. 
141. Train a model with an AUC-first objective (rank separation).  
142. Select an operating point by solving a constrained threshold choice on a calibration fold (not on the test slice), e.g., maximize macro F1 subject to platform recall constraint, or minimize FP subject to recall constraint.  
143. Optionally use a method with finite-sample error control framing (Neyman–Pearson umbrella). citeturn6search8turn6search0
144. 
145. This is also where ranking-focused models may help: if rank separation becomes strong, then there exists a wider range of thresholds that satisfy both constraints.
146. 
147. ## Evaluation governance and concrete next-cycle experiment program
148. 
149. ### Why governance matters with small holdouts
150. 
151. When the scored holdout is tiny, single-point differences (e.g., AUC 0.65 vs 0.66) may not be meaningful without uncertainty quantification. DeLong’s method is a classic non-parametric approach for comparing correlated ROC AUC curves and constructing variance estimates. citeturn11search2turn11search6  
152. Bootstrap approaches provide an alternative for confidence intervals, and are widely used in practice. citeturn11search1turn11search17  
153. At the same time, there are known pitfalls when comparing nested models with DeLong-like tests if assumptions are violated; governance should define which comparisons are legitimate and how to interpret them. citeturn11search5
154. 
155. This supports a next-cycle governance recommendation: define “pass” as “point estimate above threshold *and* lower CI bound above threshold,” or define a “near-pass window” when the CI overlaps the threshold and the error guardrails are satisfied.
156. 
157. ### Prioritized experiment designs
158. 
159. The designs below are *recipes*, not execution instructions. They assume a repo structure with `benchmarks/` scripts and `outputs/` artifacts (adapt file paths to your repo conventions).

59. def _session_type_for_source_video(source_video_path: str) -> SessionTypeInfo:

72. def _event_label_for_row(session_type: str, row: dict[str, Any]) -> tuple[str, str, bool]:
73.     review_label = str(row.get("review_label") or "")
74.     subtype = str(row.get("subtype") or "")
75.     human_label = str(row.get("human_label") or "")
76.     if review_label == "dive" or human_label == "dive":
77.         if session_type == "springboard":
78.             return "springboard_dive", "session_type_inferred", False
79.         if session_type == "platform":
80.             return "platform_dive", "session_type_inferred", False
81.         return "platform_dive", "uncertain", True
82.     if review_label == "non_dive" and subtype == "board_rebound":
83.         return "springboard_rebound_only", "subtype_mapped", False
84.     if review_label == "non_dive" and subtype in {"voice_whistle", "handling_noise", "non_dive_splash"}:
85.         return "noise_or_other", "subtype_mapped", False
86.     if review_label == "non_dive" and not subtype:
87.         return "noise_or_other", "uncertain", True
88.     if review_label == "false_negative" or human_label == "dive":
89.         if session_type == "springboard":
90.             return "springboard_dive", "session_type_inferred", False
91.         if session_type == "platform":
92.             return "platform_dive", "session_type_inferred", False
93.         return "platform_dive", "uncertain", True
94.     return "noise_or_other", "uncertain", True

97. def _anchor_timestamp(row: dict[str, Any]) -> float:

122. def _manifest_row(
123.     *,
124.     source_root: str,
125.     source_session_id: str,
126.     source_video_path: str,
127.     session_type_info: SessionTypeInfo,
128.     row: dict[str, Any],
129.     is_false_negative: bool,
130.     anchor_strategy: str,
131. ) -> dict[str, Any]:
132.     event_label, event_label_provenance, uncertainty = _event_label_for_row(session_type_info.session_type, row)
133.     proposal_timestamp = float(row.get("proposal_timestamp_seconds") or row.get("timestamp_seconds") or row.get("timestamp") or _anchor_timestamp(row))
134.     anchor_timestamp = proposal_timestamp
135.     window_pre = 0.75 if anchor_strategy == PRIMARY_ANCHOR_STRATEGY else 1.0
136.     window_post = 2.25 if anchor_strategy == PRIMARY_ANCHOR_STRATEGY else 3.0
137.     if is_false_negative:
138.         anchor_timestamp = float(row.get("timestamp_seconds") or row.get("timestamp") or anchor_timestamp)
139.     elif session_type_info.session_type == "springboard":
140.         anchor_timestamp = max(0.0, proposal_timestamp - SPRINGBOARD_STRONG_PEAK_OFFSET_SECONDS)
141.     else:
142.         anchor_timestamp = proposal_timestamp
143.     return {
144.         "source_session_root": source_root,
145.         "source_session_id": source_session_id,
146.         "source_video_path": source_video_path,
147.         "session_type": session_type_info.session_type,
148.         "session_type_provenance": session_type_info.provenance,
149.         "session_type_confidence": session_type_info.confidence,
150.         "legacy_candidate_id": row.get("source_candidate_id") or row.get("detectionId") or row.get("proposal_id"),
151.         "legacy_candidate_label": row.get("review_label") or row.get("label") or row.get("human_label"),
152.         "legacy_non_dive_subtype": row.get("subtype"),
153.         "is_false_negative_window": bool(is_false_negative),
154.         "event_anchor_timestamp_seconds": anchor_timestamp,
155.         "anchor_strategy": "earliest_strong_peak_in_local_cluster" if session_type_info.session_type == "springboard" else PRIMARY_ANCHOR_STRATEGY,
156.         "event_window_start_seconds": max(0.0, anchor_timestamp - window_pre),
157.         "event_window_end_seconds": anchor_timestamp + window_post,
158.         "event_label": event_label,
159.         "event_label_provenance": event_label_provenance,
160.         "uncertainty_flag": bool(uncertainty),
161.         **_legacy_scores(row),
162.     }

183.

217.                 "reviewed_candidates": len(reviewed_candidates),

219.             }
220.         )
221. 
222.     summary = {

31. def _load_decisions(review_path: Path) -> dict[str, dict[str, Any]]:
32.     store = read_json(review_path) or {"decisions": [], "falseNegatives": []}
33.     decisions = {}
34.     for row in store.get("decisions", []):
35.         detection_id = str(row.get("detectionId") or "")
36.         if detection_id:

38.     return decisions

41. def _final_event_label(decision: dict[str, Any] | None) -> tuple[str | None, str | None, bool]:
42.     if not decision:
43.         return None, None, False
44.     event_label = decision.get("eventLabel")
45.     if not event_label:
46.         return None, None, False
47.     return str(event_label), "human_reviewed", True
48. 
49. 
50. def build_reviewed_manifest(session_path: str, output_dir: str | None) -> tuple[list[dict[str, Any]], dict[str, Any]]:
51.     paths = resolve_evaluation_session_paths(session_path)
52.     manifest = read_json(paths["manifest_path"])
53.     if not manifest:
54.         raise FileNotFoundError(f"Could not read session manifest: {paths['manifest_path']}")
55.     export_dir = Path(str(paths["output_dir"]))
56.     event_support_rows = _load_event_support(export_dir)
57.     decisions = _load_decisions(Path(str(paths["output_dir"])) / "evaluation_review.json")
58.     source_root = str(Path(session_path).resolve())
59.     rows: list[dict[str, Any]] = []
60.     for row in event_support_rows:
61.         legacy_candidate_id = str(row.get("legacy_candidate_id") or "")
62.         decision = decisions.get(legacy_candidate_id) if legacy_candidate_id else None
63.         final_event_label, final_provenance, human_reviewed = _final_event_label(decision)
64.         rows.append(
65.             {
66.                 "source_session_root": source_root,
67.                 "source_session_id": manifest["session"]["id"],
68.                 "source_video_path": manifest["session"]["source_video_path"],
69.                 "session_type": row.get("suggested_session_type_context"),
70.                 "session_type_provenance": row.get("session_type_provenance"),
71.                 "legacy_candidate_id": row.get("legacy_candidate_id"),
72.                 "legacy_decision_label": row.get("legacy_candidate_label"),
73.                 "legacy_subtype": row.get("legacy_non_dive_subtype"),
74.                 "suggested_event_label": row.get("suggested_event_label"),
75.                 "suggested_event_label_confidence": row.get("suggested_event_label_confidence"),
76.                 "suggested_event_label_reason": row.get("suggested_event_label_reason"),
77.                 "has_preceding_rebound_context": row.get("has_preceding_rebound_context"),
78.                 "has_delayed_entry_candidate": row.get("has_delayed_entry_candidate"),
79.                 "no_rebound_context_detected": row.get("no_rebound_context_detected"),
80.                 "event_window_start_seconds": row.get("event_window_start_seconds"),
81.                 "event_window_end_seconds": row.get("event_window_end_seconds"),
82.                 "final_human_event_label": final_event_label,
83.                 "final_human_event_label_provenance": final_provenance,
84.                 "human_reviewed_at_event_level": human_reviewed,
85.                 "review_decision_label": decision.get("label") if decision else None,
86.                 "review_subtype": decision.get("subtype") if decision else None,
87.                 "review_notes": decision.get("notes") if decision else None,
88.                 "legacy_decision_human_reviewed": decision is not None,
89.             }
90.         )
91. 
92.     summary = {
93.         "session_id": manifest["session"]["id"],
94.         "row_count": len(rows),
95.         "reviewed_count": sum(1 for row in rows if row.get("human_reviewed_at_event_level")),
96.         "missing_event_label_count": sum(1 for row in rows if not row.get("final_human_event_label")),
97.         "final_label_counts": dict(Counter(str(row.get("final_human_event_label")) for row in rows if row.get("final_human_event_label"))),
98.         "legacy_label_counts": dict(Counter(str(row.get("legacy_decision_label")) for row in rows)),
99.         "agreement_counts": {
100.             "agree": sum(
101.                 1
102.                 for row in rows
103.                 if row.get("final_human_event_label")
104.                 and str(row.get("final_human_event_label")) == str(row.get("suggested_event_label"))
105.             ),
106.             "disagree": sum(
107.                 1
108.                 for row in rows
109.                 if row.get("final_human_event_label")
110.                 and str(row.get("final_human_event_label")) != str(row.get("suggested_event_label"))
111.             ),
112.         },
113.         "source_root": source_root,
114.     }
115.     return rows, summary

118. def write_preview_md(path: Path, summary: dict[str, Any], rows: Sequence[dict[str, Any]]) -> Path:
119.     lines = [
120.         "# Event Reviewed Manifest Preview",
121.         "",
122.         f"- session: `{summary['session_id']}`",
123.         f"- rows: `{summary['row_count']}`",
124.         f"- reviewed rows: `{summary['reviewed_count']}`",
125.         f"- missing final event labels: `{summary['missing_event_label_count']}`",
126.         "",
127.         "## Counts",
128.         "",
129.         f"- final labels: `{json.dumps(summary['final_label_counts'], sort_keys=True)}`",
130.         f"- legacy labels: `{json.dumps(summary['legacy_label_counts'], sort_keys=True)}`",
131.         f"- suggestion agreement: `{json.dumps(summary['agreement_counts'], sort_keys=True)}`",
132.         "",
133.         "## Example Reviewed Rows",
134.         "",
135.     ]
136.     for row in rows[:5]:
137.         lines.append(
138.             f"- `{row.get('legacy_candidate_id')}` -> final `{row.get('final_human_event_label')}` / suggestion `{row.get('suggested_event_label')}`"
139.         )
140.     lines.append("")
141.     lines.extend([
142.         "## Notes",
143.         "",
144.         "- final event labels are human-reviewed values from the desktop review store",
145.         "- legacy detector decisions and suggestion fields are preserved",
146.         "- missing rows remain visible for dataset completeness tracking",
147.     ])
148.     path.parent.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)
149.     path.write_text("\n".join(lines) + "\n", encoding="utf-8")
150.     return path
151. 
152. 
153. def main(argv: Sequence[str] | None = None) -> int:
154.     args = build_parser().parse_args(list(argv or []))
155.     rows, summary = build_reviewed_manifest(args.session_path, args.output_dir or None)
156.     paths = resolve_evaluation_session_paths(args.session_path)
157.     output_dir = Path(args.output_dir).expanduser().resolve() if args.output_dir else Path(str(paths["output_dir"])) / DEFAULT_OUTPUT_ROOT
158.     output_dir.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)
159.     json_path = output_dir / "event_reviewed_manifest.jsonl"
160.     md_path = output_dir / "event_reviewed_manifest_summary.md"
161.     write_jsonl(json_path, rows)
162.     write_preview_md(md_path, summary, rows)
163.     write_json(Path(args.preview_json), summary)
164.     write_preview_md(Path(args.preview_md), summary, rows)
165.     print(json.dumps({"json_path": str(json_path), "md_path": str(md_path), "summary": summary}, indent=2, default=str))
166.     return 0

1. # Event Window Manifest Spec
2. 
3. Date: 2026-04-11
4. 
5. ## Purpose
6. 
7. This spec defines the preview manifest layer for the next event-aware architecture.
8. 
9. The manifest layer reuses the existing evaluation/review/export workflow as the extraction backbone, but it does not rewrite legacy detector semantics.
10. 
11. Legacy labels remain preserved as legacy metadata.
12. 
13. New event-window labels are added separately.
14. 
15. ## Scope
16. 
17. This spec covers:
18. 
19. - event-window manifest row shape
20. - label mapping rules
21. - provenance handling
22. - anchor and window metadata
23. - preview export behavior
24. 
25. This spec does not cover:
26. 
27. - model training
28. - detector changes
29. - threshold changes
30. - live integration
31. 
32. ## 1. Manifest Source Inputs
33. 
34. The preview exporter should consume existing evaluated/reviewed session artifacts:
35. 
36. - `ui_session_manifest.json`
37. - `evaluation_review.json`
38. - `exports/evaluation-review/reviewed_candidates.jsonl`
39. - `exports/evaluation-review/false_negatives.jsonl`
40. - optional supporting proposal diagnostics where available
41. 
42. The exporter must treat these as source metadata, not as a replacement for event labels.
43. 
44. ## 2. Manifest Row Contract
45. 
46. Each manifest row must contain the following minimum fields.
47. 
48. ### 2.1 Session Identity
49. 
50. - `source_session_root`
51. - `source_session_id`
52. - `source_video_path`
53. - `session_type`
54. - `session_type_provenance`
55. - `session_type_confidence`
56. 
57. ### 2.2 Legacy Review Metadata
58. 
59. - `legacy_candidate_id`
60. - `legacy_candidate_label`
61. - `legacy_non_dive_subtype`
62. - `is_false_negative_window`
63. 
64. ### 2.3 Event Window Metadata
65. 
66. - `event_anchor_timestamp_seconds`
67. - `anchor_strategy`
68. - `event_window_start_seconds`
69. - `event_window_end_seconds`
70. - `event_label`
71. - `event_label_provenance`
72. - `uncertainty_flag`
73. 
74. ### 2.4 Legacy Detector Metadata
75. 
76. - `proposal_timestamp_seconds`
77. - `proposal_frontend`
78. - `clip_probability`
79. - `audio_score`
80. - `combined_score`
81. - `audio_model_probability`
82. - `audio_clip_probability`
83. - `raw_proposal_score`
84. - `threshold_passed`
85. 
86. ### 2.5 Compatibility Rule
87. 
88. Legacy metadata must remain intact.
89. 
90. The exporter may add new event-level fields, but it must not:
91. 
92. - overwrite legacy review labels in place
93. - reinterpret existing subtype strings as direct event truth
94. - drop uncertainty
95. 
96. ## 3. Event Taxonomy
97. 
98. The first preview manifest must use the Phase 2 taxonomy exactly:
99. 
100. 1. `springboard_dive`
101. 2. `springboard_rebound_only`
102. 3. `platform_dive`
103. 4. `noise_or_other`
104. 
105. Operational meaning:
106. 
107. - `springboard_dive`: springboard-origin dive event window with rebound structure and delayed entry
108. - `springboard_rebound_only`: springboard-origin non-dive event dominated by rebound structure
109. - `platform_dive`: platform-origin dive event window with weak or diffuse onset and late entry
110. - `noise_or_other`: non-dive clutter or negative event window that is not a rebound-only springboard event
111. 
112. ## 4. Provenance Rules
113. 
114. Each row must carry exactly one explicit provenance tag for the event label:
115. 
116. - `direct_review`
117. - `session_type_inferred`
118. - `subtype_mapped`
119. - `uncertain`
120. 
121. ### 4.1 `direct_review`
122. 
123. Use when the event label is directly supported by human review without type conversion or subtype mapping.
124. 
125. ### 4.2 `session_type_inferred`
126. 
127. Use when a reviewed `dive` label is mapped to `springboard_dive` or `platform_dive` from session type knowledge.
128. 
129. This must not be silently promoted to direct truth.
130. 
131. ### 4.3 `subtype_mapped`
132. 
133. Use when a reviewed non-dive subtype is mapped into the event taxonomy.
134. 
135. Examples:
136. 
137. - `board_rebound` -> `springboard_rebound_only`
138. - `voice_whistle` -> `noise_or_other`
139. - `handling_noise` -> `noise_or_other`
140. - `non_dive_splash` -> `noise_or_other`
141. 
142. ### 4.4 `uncertain`
143. 
144. Use when the row cannot be assigned confidently from current evidence.
145. 
146. `uncertain` rows must remain visible in counts and summaries.
147. 
148. ## 5. Session-Type Rules
149. 
150. The exporter must attach a session type to each row.
151. 
152. Recommended initial session types:
153. 
154. - `springboard`
155. - `platform`
156. - `unknown`
157. 
158. Recommended provenance categories:
159. 
160. - `direct_review`
161. - `session_type_inferred`
162. - `uncertain`
163. 
164. Important rule:
165. 
166. - session type can be supported directly by the archived project docs for some sessions, or inferred from review context for others
167. - session type inference must not be disguised as direct review
168. 
169. Recommended session-type provenance categories:
170. 
171. - `direct_review`
172. - `session_type_inferred`
173. - `uncertain`
174. 
175. ## 6. Anchor Strategy
176. 
177. The first preview exporter should support at least:
178. 
179. 1. `proposal_centered`
180. 2. `earliest_strong_peak_in_local_cluster`
181. 
182. Recommended primary anchor:
183. 
184. - `proposal_centered`
185. 
186. Recommended backup anchor:
187. 
188. - `earliest_strong_peak_in_local_cluster`
189. 
190. Rationale:
191. 
192. - `proposal_centered` matches the intended future architecture boundary
193. - `earliest_strong_peak_in_local_cluster` is a fallback for rebound-dominated springboard clusters
194. 
195. ## 7. Window Strategy
196. 
197. The first preview exporter should emit asymmetric window boundaries.
198. 
199. Recommended primary window:
200. 
201. - `0.75s pre`
202. - `2.25s post`
203. - `3.0s total`
204. 
205. Recommended backup window:
206. 
207. - `1.0s pre`
208. - `3.0s post`
209. - `4.0s total`
210. 
211. ## 8. Preview Export Behavior
212. 
213. The initial manifest export should be a preview, not a training set.
214. 
215. It should:
216. 
217. - cover a small authoritative set of local reviewed roots
218. - preserve provenance tags
219. - materialize rows reproducibly
220. - write a JSONL manifest
221. - write a markdown summary
222. 
223. The preview should not:
224. 
225. - train a model
226. - alter detector outputs
227. - rename legacy labels
228. - fabricate direct event truth
229. 
230. ## 9. Required Output Artifacts
231. 
232. The preview export should write:
233. 
234. - `outputs/event_window_manifest_preview.jsonl`
235. - `outputs/event_window_manifest_preview_summary.md`
236. 
237. ## 10. Acceptance Criteria
238. 
239. The preview export is acceptable if:
240. 
241. - rows can be materialized from the reviewed session roots
242. - every row has a valid event label and provenance tag
243. - legacy metadata is preserved
244. - uncertainty is explicit
245. - the preview summary reports counts by event label, provenance, and session type
246. 
247. ## 11. Open Gaps
248. 
249. The preview export is not the final dataset.
250. 
251. Open gaps after Phase 3 preview:
252. 
253. - direct event-window review labels are still missing
254. - session-type certainty is still partly inferred
255. - the four-class taxonomy is still a prototype schema, not a validated dataset label set
256.
```

```
1. # Event Review Workflow Plan
2. 
3. Date: 2026-04-11
4. 
5. ## Purpose
6. 
7. This plan defines a small review-support layer for the event-window architecture.
8. 
9. The goal is reviewer efficiency and label-quality improvement.
10. 
11. This is not model training and not detector integration.
12. 
13. ## Where The New Step Fits
14. 
15. Current flow:
16. 
17. 1. `evaluate-session`
18. 2. human review in the WebUI
19. 3. `export-evaluation-review`
20. 4. downstream analysis or replay
21. 
22. Proposed flow:
23. 
24. 1. `evaluate-session`
25. 2. `export-event-review-support`
26. 3. human review in the WebUI with event hints visible
27. 4. `export-evaluation-review`
28. 5. downstream analysis or replay
29. 
30. The new step is a precompute layer after candidate detection and before review consumption.
31. 
32. It prepares event-level hints from the already-detected candidate set.
33. 
34. ## New UI-Facing Concepts
35. 
36. The UI layer needs to distinguish:
37. 
38. - legacy detector label
39. - event-level review label
40. - machine-generated suggestion
41. - provenance / confidence of the suggestion
42. - event window bounds
43. 
44. Suggested UI concepts:
45. 
46. - `suggested_event_label`
47. - `suggested_event_label_confidence`
48. - `suggested_event_label_reason`
49. - `suggested_session_type_context`
50. - `has_preceding_rebound_context`
51. - `has_delayed_entry_candidate`
52. - `event_label_provenance_suggestion`
53. - `event_anchor_strategy`
54. - `event_window_start_seconds`
55. - `event_window_end_seconds`
56. 
57. ## What Is A Suggestion Versus A Label
58. 
59. ### Suggestions
60. 
61. Suggestions are machine-generated hints only.
62. 
63. Examples:
64. 
65. - `suggested_event_label`
66. - `suggested_event_label_reason`
67. - `suggested_session_type_context`
68. - `event_label_provenance_suggestion`
69. 
70. These fields should help the reviewer decide faster.
71. 
72. They are not final truth.
73. 
74. ### Labels
75. 
76. Labels remain human-reviewed decisions.
77. 
78. Examples:
79. 
80. - legacy detector review label
81. - legacy non-dive subtype
82. - final event-window review label when that workflow is added later
83. 
84. The workflow must preserve legacy labels rather than overwriting them.
85. 
86. ## Provenance Preservation
87. 
88. The support layer should preserve both:
89. 
90. - legacy review provenance
91. - new suggestion provenance
92. 
93. Suggested provenance categories:
94. 
95. - `direct_review`
96. - `session_type_inferred`
97. - `subtype_mapped`
98. - `uncertain`
99. 
100. Suggested UI behavior:
101. 
102. - show the suggestion provenance next to the machine hint
103. - keep the human-reviewed label separate
104. - keep uncertain rows visible instead of hiding them
105. 
106. ## What The Reviewer Should Be Able To Confirm Quickly
107. 
108. The reviewer should be able to confirm:
109. 
110. - whether the candidate is a springboard dive
111. - whether the candidate is a springboard rebound-only event
112. - whether the candidate is a platform dive
113. - whether the candidate is noise or other clutter
114. - whether the proposed event window makes sense
115. - whether the suggestion should be accepted, rejected, or marked uncertain
116. 
117. The reviewer should not need to infer the detector lineage manually.
118. 
119. ## Conservative Heuristic Rules
120. 
121. The first review-support pass should stay simple:
122. 
123. - if a dive occurs after a nearby board-rebound-labeled sound, suggest `springboard_dive`
124. - if a dive occurs with no nearby rebound-like context, keep the context flag visible and only suggest `platform_dive` when the session type itself supports that interpretation
125. - if a board-rebound event has no plausible delayed entry in the event window, suggest `springboard_rebound_only`
126. - if a negative event is whistle/handling/splash-like, map it toward `noise_or_other`
127. 
128. The output should remain a hint layer, not an automated labeling system.
129. 
130. ## UI / Data Contract Impact
131. 
132. The session manifest should gain optional event-review support fields.
133. 
134. The review store should continue to persist only human decisions.
135. 
136. The UI should be able to read:
137. 
138. - legacy review data
139. - event-review support hints
140. - event window start/end markers
141. 
142. No existing review semantics should change.
143. 
144. ## Workflow Safety Rules
145. 
146. - do not change detector thresholds
147. - do not change classifier logic
148. - do not introduce live event-level scoring into the detector
149. - do not silently convert suggestions into labels
150. - do not hide provenance
151. - do not turn `no_rebound_context_detected` into a class suggestion by itself
152. 
153. ## Output Expectation
154. 
155. After the precompute step, the WebUI should have a richer artifact surface for review, but the final decision remains human-controlled.
156.
```

1. # Platform/Noise Feature-Family Design (r4)
2. 
3. ## Part D — Proposed platform/noise feature family
4. 
5. ### Design target
6. 
7. Separate:
8. - true `platform_dive`
9. from
10. - `noise_or_other`
11. 
12. while keeping detector/taxonomy/labels/springboard/model-family unchanged.
13. 
14. ### Proposed small interpretable family: `platform_noise_probe_p1_compactness_texture_decay`
15. 
16. 1. **Impact compactness**
17.    - `peak_to_window_energy_ratio`
18.    - `attack_rise_ms`
19.    - `single_peak_dominance`
20.    - Purpose: suppress handling-noise FPs by requiring compact, dominant impact structure.
21. 
22. 2. **Broadband splash decay**
23.    - `post_impact_decay_ratio_0_120ms_vs_120_600ms`
24.    - `tail_half_life_ms`
25.    - Purpose: encode impact-followed-by-decay shape expected in dives vs sustained diffuse clutter.
26. 
27. 3. **Tonal vs broadband texture**
28.    - `tonal_peak_persistence`
29.    - `spectral_flatness_post_anchor`
30.    - `whistle_band_energy_fraction`
31.    - Purpose: explicitly separate whistle-like tonal noise from broadband splash signatures.
32. 
33. 4. **Isolation vs diffuse clutter**
34.    - `transient_count_in_window`
35.    - `inter_peak_interval_cv`
36.    - Purpose: penalize multi-transient handling clutter that currently collapses into platform.
37. 
38. ### Why this is tied to r4 failures
39. 
40. - The 9 false positives are dominated by `handling_noise` and `voice_whistle`, so the missing information is shape/texture discrimination, not taxonomy.
41. - The 2 false negatives are clean legacy dives (`det-0003`, `det-0008`), so we also need features that preserve compact true-dive signatures while suppressing diffuse negatives.
42. 
43. ## Part E — Single best next action
44. 
45. **Choice: A — derive a small new platform/noise feature family and rerun the same model.**
46. 
47. ### Justification
48. 
49. - The failure mode is representation-driven (noise heterogeneity collapsing into platform), so feature repair is the minimal justified next step.
50. - Immediate model-family change would obscure root cause before testing the missing shape/texture information.
51. - Relabeling or slice revision is not justified now because the scored slice is already valid and label ambiguity is not the top-ranked cause.
52. 
53. ### Probe contract
54. 
55. - keep classifier family unchanged
56. - keep detector behavior unchanged
57. - keep taxonomy unchanged
58. - keep labels unchanged
59. - evaluate on the same frozen r4 holdout slice
60.
```

87. def framing(signal: np.ndarray, frame: int, hop: int) -> np.ndarray:
88.     if len(signal) < frame:
89.         padded = np.zeros(frame, dtype=np.float32)
90.         padded[: len(signal)] = signal
91.         return padded.reshape(1, frame)
92.     n_frames = 1 + (len(signal) - frame) // hop
93.     return np.lib.stride_tricks.as_strided(
94.         signal,
95.         shape=(n_frames, frame),
96.         strides=(signal.strides[0] * hop, signal.strides[0]),
97.         writeable=False,
98.     )
99.

101. def local_peak_indices(values: np.ndarray, threshold: float) -> np.ndarray:
102.     if len(values) < 3:
103.         return np.asarray([], dtype=int)
104.     peaks = []
105.     for i in range(1, len(values) - 1):
106.         if values[i] >= values[i - 1] and values[i] >= values[i + 1] and values[i] >= threshold:
107.             peaks.append(i)
108.     return np.asarray(peaks, dtype=int)
109.

111. def octave_band_edges(fmin: float = 200.0, n_bands: int = 6, max_freq: float = 8000.0) -> list[tuple[float, float]]:
112.     edges = []
113.     low = 0.0
114.     first_high = min(fmin, max_freq)
115.     edges.append((low, first_high))
116.     low = first_high
117.     for _ in range(n_bands):
118.         high = min(low * 2.0, max_freq)
119.         if high <= low:
120.             break
121.         edges.append((low, high))
122.         low = high
123.         if high >= max_freq:
124.             break
125.     return edges
126.

136.         mask = (freqs >= lo) & (freqs < hi)
137.         if int(np.sum(mask)) < 3:
138.             continue
139.         band = power_post[:, mask]
140.         top = np.quantile(band, 0.98, axis=1)

53. def accuracy_score(y_true: np.ndarray, y_pred: np.ndarray) -> float:

57. def confusion_matrix(y_true: np.ndarray, y_pred: np.ndarray, labels: list[str]) -> list[list[int]]:
58.     index = {label: i for i, label in enumerate(labels)}
59.     matrix = np.zeros((len(labels), len(labels)), dtype=int)
60.     for truth, pred in zip(y_true, y_pred):
61.         matrix[index[str(truth)]][index[str(pred)]] += 1
62.     return matrix.tolist()

65. def precision_recall_f1(y_true: np.ndarray, y_pred: np.ndarray, label: str) -> dict[str, float]:
66.     tp = int(np.sum((y_true == label) & (y_pred == label)))
67.     fp = int(np.sum((y_true != label) & (y_pred == label)))
68.     fn = int(np.sum((y_true == label) & (y_pred != label)))
69.     precision = tp / (tp + fp) if tp + fp else 0.0
70.     recall = tp / (tp + fn) if tp + fn else 0.0
71.     f1 = 2 * precision * recall / (precision + recall) if precision + recall else 0.0
72.     return {"precision": precision, "recall": recall, "f1": f1, "support": tp + fn}
73.

75. def macro_metrics(y_true: np.ndarray, y_pred: np.ndarray, labels: list[str]) -> dict[str, float]:
76.     prfs = [precision_recall_f1(y_true, y_pred, label) for label in labels]
77.     return {
78.         "precision": float(np.mean([item["precision"] for item in prfs])) if prfs else 0.0,
79.         "recall": float(np.mean([item["recall"] for item in prfs])) if prfs else 0.0,
80.         "f1": float(np.mean([item["f1"] for item in prfs])) if prfs else 0.0,
81.     }

84. def binary_auc(y_true: np.ndarray, scores: np.ndarray, positive_label: str) -> float:
85.     pos = scores[y_true == positive_label]
86.     neg = scores[y_true != positive_label]
87.     total = len(pos) * len(neg)
88.     if total == 0:
89.         return 0.5
90.     gt = 0
91.     eq = 0
92.     for value in pos:
93.         diff = value - neg
94.         gt += int(np.sum(diff > 0))
95.         eq += int(np.sum(diff == 0))
96.     auc = (gt + 0.5 * eq) / total
97.     return float(max(auc, 1.0 - auc))

111. def softmax(z: np.ndarray) -> np.ndarray:
112.     z = z - np.max(z, axis=1, keepdims=True)
113.     exp = np.exp(np.clip(z, -40.0, 40.0))
114.     return exp / np.maximum(exp.sum(axis=1, keepdims=True), 1e-12)

117. def train_multinomial_logreg(x: np.ndarray, y: np.ndarray, class_names: list[str], epochs: int = 1200, lr: float = 0.08, l2: float = 0.01) -> dict:
118.     n_samples, n_features = x.shape
119.     n_classes = len(class_names)
120.     weights = np.zeros((n_classes, n_features), dtype=np.float64)
121.     bias = np.zeros(n_classes, dtype=np.float64)
122.     for _ in range(epochs):
123.         logits = x @ weights.T + bias
124.         probs = softmax(logits)
125.         target = np.zeros_like(probs)
126.         target[np.arange(n_samples), y] = 1.0
127.         error = probs - target
128.         grad_w = error.T @ x / n_samples + l2 * weights
129.         grad_b = error.mean(axis=0)
130.         weights -= lr * grad_w
131.         bias -= lr * grad_b
132.     return {"weights": weights, "bias": bias, "classes": class_names}

135. def predict_multinomial(model: dict, x: np.ndarray) -> tuple[np.ndarray, np.ndarray]:
136.     logits = x @ model["weights"].T + model["bias"]
137.     probs = softmax(logits)
138.     pred = np.argmax(probs, axis=1)
139.     return pred, probs

142. def train_binary_logreg(x: np.ndarray, y: np.ndarray, epochs: int = 1000, lr: float = 0.1, l2: float = 0.01) -> dict:
143.     n_samples, n_features = x.shape
144.     weights = np.zeros(n_features, dtype=np.float64)
145.     bias = 0.0
146.     for _ in range(epochs):
147.         logits = x @ weights + bias
148.         probs = 1.0 / (1.0 + np.exp(-np.clip(logits, -40.0, 40.0)))
149.         error = probs - y
150.         grad_w = (x.T @ error) / n_samples + l2 * weights
151.         grad_b = float(np.mean(error))
152.         weights -= lr * grad_w
153.         bias -= lr * grad_b
154.     return {"weights": weights, "bias": bias}

178.         1.0 if row.get("session_type") == "springboard" else 0.0,
179.         1.0 if row.get("session_type") == "platform" else 0.0,
180.         1.0 if row.get("event_label_provenance") == "session_type_inferred" else 0.0,
181.         1.0 if row.get("event_label_provenance") == "subtype_mapped" else 0.0,
182.         1.0 if row.get("event_label_provenance") == "uncertain" else 0.0,
183.     ]
184. 
185. 
186. def collect_dataset(rows: list[dict], strict: bool) -> list[dict]:
187.     selected = []
188.     for row in rows:
189.         if strict:
190.             if row.get("session_type_provenance") != "direct_review":
191.                 continue
192.         else:
193.             if event_label_for_row(row) is None:
194.                 continue
195.         selected.append(row)
196.     return selected
197. 
198. 
199. def split_by_session(rows: list[dict]) -> list[tuple[str, list[dict], list[dict]]]:
200.     by_session: dict[str, list[dict]] = defaultdict(list)
201.     for row in rows:
202.         by_session[str(row["source_session_id"])].append(row)
203.     sessions = sorted(by_session)
204.     splits = []
205.     for held_out in sessions:
206.         train = [row for sid, subset in by_session.items() if sid != held_out for row in subset]
207.         test = list(by_session[held_out])
208.         splits.append((held_out, train, test))
209.     return splits
210. 
211. 
212. def train_eval_four_class(train_rows: list[dict], test_rows: list[dict], labels: list[str]) -> dict:
213.     x_train = np.asarray([feature_vector(row) for row in train_rows], dtype=np.float64)
214.     x_test = np.asarray([feature_vector(row) for row in test_rows], dtype=np.float64)
215.     y_train = np.asarray([labels.index(event_label_for_row(row)) for row in train_rows], dtype=int)
216.     y_test = np.asarray([labels.index(event_label_for_row(row)) for row in test_rows], dtype=int)
217.     mean, std = standardize_fit(x_train)
218.     x_train = standardize_apply(x_train, mean, std)
219.     x_test = standardize_apply(x_test, mean, std)
220.     model = train_multinomial_logreg(x_train, y_train, labels)
```

## Overview[](#overview "Link to this heading")

Often in the context of information retrieval, learning-to-rank aims to train a model that arranges a set of query results into an ordered list [\[1\]](#references). For supervised learning-to-rank, the predictors are sample documents encoded as feature matrix, and the labels are relevance degree for each sample. Relevance degree can be multi-level (graded) or binary (relevant or not). The training samples are often grouped by their query index with each query group containing multiple query results.

XGBoost implements learning to rank through a set of objective functions and performance metrics. The default objective is `rank:ndcg` based on the `LambdaMART` [\[2\]](#references) algorithm, which in turn is an adaptation of the `LambdaRank` [\[3\]](#references) framework to gradient boosting trees. For a history and a summary of the algorithm, see [\[5\]](#references). The implementation in XGBoost features deterministic GPU computation, distributed training, position debiasing and two different pair construction strategies.

## Training with the Pairwise Objective[](#training-with-the-pairwise-objective "Link to this heading")

`LambdaMART` is a pairwise ranking model, meaning that it compares the relevance degree for every pair of samples in a query group and calculate a proxy gradient for each pair. The default objective `rank:ndcg` is using the surrogate gradient derived from the `ndcg` metric. To train a XGBoost model, we need an additional sorted array called `qid` for specifying the query group of input samples. An example input would look like this:

QID

Label

Features

1

0

\\(x\_1\\)

1

1

\\(x\_2\\)

1

0

\\(x\_3\\)

2

0

\\(x\_4\\)

2

1

\\(x\_5\\)

2

1

\\(x\_6\\)

2

1

\\(x\_7\\)

Notice that the samples are sorted based on their query index in a non-decreasing order. In the above example, the first three samples belong to the first query and the next four samples belong to the second. For the sake of simplicity, we will use a synthetic binary learning-to-rank dataset in the following code snippets, with binary labels representing whether the result is relevant or not, and randomly assign the query group index to each sample. For an example that uses a real world dataset, please see [Getting started with learning to rank](../python/examples/learning_to_rank.html#sphx-glr-python-examples-learning-to-rank-py).

from sklearn.datasets import make\_classification
import numpy as np

import xgboost as xgb

\# Make a synthetic ranking dataset for demonstration
seed \= 1994
X, y \= make\_classification(random\_state\=seed)
rng \= np.random.default\_rng(seed)
n\_query\_groups \= 3
qid \= rng.integers(0, n\_query\_groups, size\=X.shape\[0\])

\# Sort the inputs based on query index
sorted\_idx \= np.argsort(qid)
X \= X\[sorted\_idx, :\]
y \= y\[sorted\_idx\]
qid \= qid\[sorted\_idx\]

The simplest way to train a ranking model is by using the scikit-learn estimator interface. Continuing the previous snippet, we can train a simple ranking model without tuning:

ranker \= xgb.XGBRanker(tree\_method\="hist", lambdarank\_num\_pair\_per\_sample\=8, objective\="rank:ndcg", lambdarank\_pair\_method\="topk")
ranker.fit(X, y, qid\=qid)

Please note that, as of writing, there’s no learning-to-rank interface in scikit-learn. As a result, the [`xgboost.XGBRanker`](../python/python_api.html#xgboost.XGBRanker "xgboost.XGBRanker") class does not fully conform the scikit-learn estimator guideline and can not be directly used with some of its utility functions. For instances, the `auc_score` and `ndcg_score` in scikit-learn don’t consider query group information nor the pairwise loss. Most of the metrics are implemented as part of XGBoost, but to use scikit-learn utilities like `sklearn.model_selection.cross_validation()`, we need to make some adjustments in order to pass the `qid` as an additional parameter for [`xgboost.XGBRanker.score()`](../python/python_api.html#xgboost.XGBRanker.score "xgboost.XGBRanker.score"). Given a data frame `X` (either pandas or cuDF), add the column `qid` as follows:

import pandas as pd

\# \`X\`, \`qid\`, and \`y\` are from the previous snippet, they are all sorted by the \`sorted\_idx\`.
df \= pd.DataFrame(X, columns\=\[str(i) for i in range(X.shape\[1\])\])
df\["qid"\] \= qid

ranker.fit(df, y)  \# No need to pass qid as a separate argument
